This section supersedes any local government regulations on matters covered under this part, including, but not limited to, the screening process used by a landlord in approving tenancies; security deposits; rental agreement applications and fees associated with such applications; terms and conditions of rental agreements; the rights and responsibilities of the landlord and tenant; disclosures concerning the premises, the dwelling unit, the rental agreement, or the rights and responsibilities of the landlord and tenant; fees charged by the landlord; or notice requirements.
3. TERM. This tenancy begins on August 1, 2025 and continues from month to month until ended by Tenant or Landlord.

10. ENTIRE AGREEMENT. This lease is the whole agreement. It may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant.

Landlord: Marsh Creek Property Management, LLC, by Dana Ortiz, Property Manager    Date: July 10, 2025
Tenant: Jordan Reyes    Date: July 10, 2025
7. NOTICES TO LANDLORD. Written notices to Landlord shall be delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, Gainesville, Florida 32608, or sent there by certified mail.

answer:
I can't say yet that this is retaliation. Your facts fit part of the retaliation law, but other parts depend on your landlord's reason, and a court decides that. Whether the increase works at all is also not settled. The law has no rule on how much notice a rent increase needs. It also doesn't say whether a landlord can raise month-to-month rent without your agreement. You have three choices, and each has a risk. You can pay the new rent, pay the old rent and explain why in writing, or end the tenancy by written notice. The last day to give that notice for the end of March is March 1, 2026. Whatever you choose, don't stop paying rent altogether.

Does the letter give a reason for the increase, or has anyone at the office told you why?

DETAILS

### Does Florida limit this rent increase or require a certain notice?
- Part II has no section that sets how much notice a rent increase needs. It also has no section that caps how much rent can go up.
- Your lease is month to month (§3). It has no clause that lets the landlord change the rent during the tenancy.
- Clause 10 says the lease "may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant." You told me you did not agree and signed nothing.
- Local rent rules can't fill the gap. The law leaves these matters to the state (83.425), and I found no state rent rule.

### Did the letter work as a rent increase?
The law is not settled here. There are three readings.
- **Reading one:** A landlord who can end a month-to-month tenancy only on 30 days' written notice (83.57(3)) can change the rent only on the same notice. The notice must be delivered a way 83.56(4) names, and "delivering a true copy" is one of them. Your landlord handed you the letter on February 20, which is before March 1. Under this reading the letter was in time for the April 1 start.
- **Reading two:** No section sets a notice for an increase, so none in particular is needed. You can pay the new rent or leave.
- **Reading three:** Section 83.57 only lets a party end the tenancy. The rent changes only if you agree. A landlord who wants more would have to end the tenancy on proper notice and offer new terms. Your lease's signed-changes clause (§10) supports this reading.

Under every reading, the landlord can end a month-to-month tenancy with written notice under 83.57. The statute names no reason for this.

### Does your mold complaint count as retaliation?
The law says it is unlawful to "discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent … primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant" (83.64(1)). All of these must be met:
1. **Something you did first.** A complaint to a code enforcement agency is named in 83.64(1)(a). Your complaint to city code enforcement about mold on January 15 fits. This part is likely met.
2. **Good faith.** You must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)). The law defines that as "honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned" (83.43(8)). A court applies this. A real mold complaint points toward good faith.
3. **Treated differently.** The law says "discrimination" means "treated differently as to the rent charged" (83.64(4)), and this is required. You say your neighbors report no change to their rent. That points toward different treatment. Your information comes from your neighbors, not from the landlord's records. It is worth confirming.
4. **Primarily to retaliate.** This is the landlord's motive, and a court decides it. An increase that came after your complaint is not retaliation for that reason alone. The landlord may have another reason.

### What can you do about it now?
- The retaliation law says you can raise it "as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession" (83.64(2)). A defense only matters once the landlord sues to evict you.
- It is not settled whether you can act before any case. One reading is that 83.64(2) makes it only a defense, so there is nothing to raise yet. The other reading is that the increase is itself unlawful under 83.64(1), and "Any right or duty declared in this part is enforceable by civil action" (83.54). That reading would allow a damages claim under 83.55.
- The defense can weaken if you stop paying. The law says it does not apply if "the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause," and it lists "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" as an example (83.64(3)).

### What are your three choices, and what does each risk?
- **Pay the new $1,400.** Whether this gives up your objection is not settled. One reading is that paying with knowledge waives a claim for those months (83.56(5)(a)) and may show you agreed. The other reading is that an increase the lease never allowed is not rent "due" (83.43(12)). Under that reading you could claim the extra back, and each later month is a new noncompliance.
- **Pay the old $1,050 and say in writing why.** Quote lease §3 and §10. The lease says to hand-deliver notices to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or send them there by certified mail (§7). Keep a copy and proof of each payment. The risk is that the landlord treats the gap as unpaid rent. A 3-day written demand for rent or possession can follow (83.56(3)). Don't ignore one. The landlord can only remove you through a court case (83.59(3)). If a case is filed, you must pay the rent into the court registry or file a motion about the amount within 5 days of service, not counting weekends and holidays (83.60(2)). If you don't, you lose your defenses except payment. The summons will state the requirement.
- **End the tenancy by written notice.** For the monthly period ending March 31, the last day to give 30 days' notice is March 1, 2026. If you miss that date, the last day for the period ending April 30 is March 31, 2026. The notice must follow 83.56(4). Whether a late notice works for the next period is not settled.

tool_calls.name: load_skill
tool_calls.result:
Loaded rent_increased. Its instructions:

# Rent increased

Rests on 83.46 (rent, tenancies with no set term), 83.43 (what rent is, good faith), 83.57 (ending a tenancy with no set term), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.425 (local rules), 83.56 (unpaid rent, rent paid, notices), 83.60 (if sued), 83.55 and 83.54 (damages, suits), 83.44 and 83.45 (good faith, unfair clauses), 83.48 (attorney fees), 83.51 and 83.491 (trash, a fee in place of a deposit), 83.59 and 83.67 (no lockout), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes"). Every point marked not settled gets all its readings, and you choose none. When the tenant asks "can I" and the answer turns on such a point, write "You can if X, and X is not settled", never a plain yes.

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- Part II has no section that sets how much notice a rent increase needs, and none that limits how much rent may go up. Say so plainly when asked. Never state a notice period or a cap as the law.
- Local rules: "The regulation of residential tenancies, the landlord-tenant relationship, and all other matters covered under this part are preempted to the state." (83.425), and the section supersedes local rules on matters including "fees charged by the landlord; or notice requirements." (83.425). The stored text holds no local rent rule. Never apply one from memory.
- Rent paid through a program (a voucher, public housing): the program's own rules are not stored. Say they may limit this, and that they are outside this tool.
- The increase comes with an offer to renew, or the tenant would rather leave: load lease_ending too.

## What the lease adds

Read the whole lease, addenda included, for: the rent, the term, any clause on the rent changing, how the lease may be changed, any charges, staying after the end, and how notices go to the landlord. Quote each clause and cite it.

- **Rent steps set in the lease from the start** (so much until a date, then more): that is the lease's rent, not an increase. Say so.
- **A clause letting the landlord raise the rent during the term:** set the increase beside the clause's conditions (how much notice, how it is given, how much, how often). If it gives a number of days N: the last day to give notice for the start date named is count_days(new_rent_starts, -N), and the earliest start from the notice given is count_days(increase_delivered, N). All conditions met: the rent goes up as the lease says; say so plainly. Any not met: the clause does not support this increase on these terms; say so plainly. The rent stays where it is for now and the tenant keeps paying it, but the landlord can still raise it by meeting the clause, so say that too. Option 1's plain answer is for a lease with no such clause. A clause with no limit at all: say what it says, that it carries "an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement." (83.44), and that whether it is unfair enough to be "unconscionable" (83.45(1)) is for a court.
- **A new charge** (an amenity fee, a trash fee): the same questions as for rent. The lease provides it: owed as the lease says. It does not: during a set term the landlord cannot add it alone, any more than it can raise the rent. A fee counts as rent only if it is "designated as rent in a written rental agreement." (83.43(12)). That matters because a demand under 83.56(3) and the registry under 83.60(2) speak of rent.
  - Trash: in a unit other than a single-family home or duplex, "Garbage removal and outside receptacles therefor." (83.51(2)(a)) falls to the landlord "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)), though the rental agreement may put the charges on the tenant (83.51(2)(e)).
  - A fee in place of a security deposit: "The amount of the fee, which may not be increased during the term of the rental agreement." (83.491(4)(a)).

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- new_rent: the new amount. increase_delivered: the date word of it reached them, and how it came (handed over, mail, portal, text, spoken). new_rent_starts: the date it is said to start.
- lease_end_date: the date the lease ends, if it has one. period_end: the last day of the rent period before the new rent starts. next_period_end: the last day of the rent period after that.
- agreed: whether they signed anything or said yes. paid_new_rent: whether they have paid the new amount, for which months, and what they knew about the lease when they paid.
- complaint_date: the date of any complaint or similar step before the increase, and what it was. others_rent: what they know about other tenants' rent.
- rent_demand: any written demand for rent, and its date. eviction_filed: whether a case has been filed, and whether they were served.

## Which kind of increase

Settle this first. With a set end date, call count_days(lease_end_date, 0) and set new_rent_starts beside the date it gives.

- A set end date, and the new rent starts on or before it: option 1.
- A set end date, and the new rent starts after it: option 2.
- No set end date, or the tenant stayed on after a set term with the landlord's permission: option 3. With no term stated, "the duration is determined by the periods for which the rent is payable." (83.46(2)). Stayed on without permission, or in doubt: load lease_ending too.

Any kind: option 4 if the tenant did something first that the landlord may be answering, such as a complaint or joining a tenant group, and the two parts after it if they fit.

## Option 1: during a set term

Part II has no section that lets a landlord raise the rent during a set term. The rent is what the lease says. Quote the rent clause and any clause on changing the lease.

1. **No clause allows it** (see "What the lease adds").
2. **The tenant did not agree.**
   - They signed a change: the rent is what they signed, if it meets the lease's clause on changes.
   - They said yes without signing: not settled whether that changes the rent. One: a rental agreement can include an "oral agreement for a duration of less than 1 year" (83.43(13)). The other: a lease clause requiring a signed change still governs.
   - They paid it without signing: this option's plain answer does not apply. Start from "If the tenant already paid it", which is not settled.

Both met: the landlord cannot change the rent alone before the lease ends. Say so plainly. The tenant keeps paying the lease's rent, in full and on time, and can tell the landlord in writing that they do not agree, quoting the rent clause and sending it the way the lease's notice clause says. It helps to keep the letter, the lease, and proof of each payment. Say the risk too: see "If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent". The landlord can ask for more when the term ends (option 2).

## Option 2: a higher rent for a new term

Part II names no right to renew at the same rent and no limit on what a landlord may ask for a new term. Say so plainly. The lease's rent stands through lease_end_date whatever the offer says. From there:

- **Agree:** the new rent starts with the new term. Say what they should read before signing: the rent, the term, and any new charge.
- **Leave at the end:** load lease_ending for any notice the lease asks for.
- **Stay without agreeing:** load lease_ending. Staying without permission can mean "double the amount of rent due" (83.58). Read the lease's clause on staying after the end; if it makes the tenancy month to month, say what it says, and option 3 applies from then.

## Option 3: no set end date

Part II sets no notice for this and does not say a landlord may change the rent alone, so what an increase takes is not settled. Give all three readings and choose none. Quote any lease clause on signed changes.

- One: a landlord that can end the tenancy only on 83.57's notice can change the rent only with the same notice, written and delivered a way 83.56(4) names, for month to month "not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)).
- Two: no section sets a notice, so none in particular is needed, and the tenant can pay it or leave.
- Three: 83.57 only lets a party end the tenancy, so the rent changes only if the tenant agrees, and a landlord that wants more must end the tenancy on that notice and offer new terms.

The date: count_days(period_end, -N), with N from 83.57: 30 for month to month (83.57(3)), and for other rent periods the number in 83.57(1), (2), or (4). Set increase_delivered beside it. The ways 83.56(4) names are mailing, a true copy by hand, e-mail under the signed addendum in 83.505(1), or, if the tenant is away, a copy left at the home.

- In writing, a way named, and on or before that date: in time under readings one and two. Say so plainly. Under reading three the letter alone still does not change the rent.
- Later than that, or spoken, or by text or portal: not good for that date under reading one, enough under reading two, and no change under reading three. Whether a late notice works for the next period under reading one is not settled, as lease_ending says of a late notice to end a tenancy; its date is count_days(next_period_end, -N).

Under every reading the landlord may end the tenancy on that notice: it "may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4)" (83.57), and no reason is named. Say so, so the tenant knows what refusing can lead to.

The short answer here: say it is not settled, then write "You have three choices, and each has a risk", then name the three below without choosing one. In the details, say what each one risks.

- Pay the new rent. Whether paying gives anything up is not settled; give both readings from "If the tenant already paid it", never one as the law.
- Pay the old rent and say in writing why. See "If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent".
- End the tenancy by written notice. Give the last day here, with the other choices: count_days(period_end, -N), or count_days(next_period_end, -N) if that has passed. Then load lease_ending for how the notice goes.

## Option 4: retaliation

"It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)).

All of these must be met.

1. **Something the tenant did first.** "Examples of conduct for which the landlord may not retaliate include, but are not limited to, situations where:" (83.64(1)) they complained to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)), took part in a tenant organization (83.64(1)(b)), complained to the landlord under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)), ended a lease as a servicemember (83.64(1)(d)), paid rent to an association after its demand (83.64(1)(e)), or used fair housing rights (83.64(1)(f)). Fair housing law itself is outside this tool. Another step, like an ordinary repair request: not settled. One: the list is only examples, so it can count. The other: it counts only if it is like the named ones, and a request that says nothing about ending the lease is not 83.56(1)'s complaint.
2. **Good faith** (83.64(1)). "“Good faith” means honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned." (83.43(8)). Applying that is for a court.
3. **Treated differently.** "“Discrimination” under this section means that a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord, which shall be a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct." (83.64(4)). Set what they know of other tenants' rent beside the words. The same increase for everyone points against it; say so plainly. If they do not know, say that is the fact to find out.
4. **Primarily to retaliate.** This is the landlord's motive, for a court. An increase that followed such a step is not retaliation for that reason alone. Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

What it gives: "Evidence of retaliatory conduct may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." (83.64(2)), unless "the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)), whose examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)). So not paying the new rent can weaken it; say so.

What the tenant can do about an increase alone, before any case: not settled. One: 83.64(2) makes it only a defense, so there is nothing to raise until a case. The other: 83.64(1) makes the increase unlawful, "Any right or duty declared in this part is enforceable by civil action." (83.54), and a party may recover damages for a failure to comply with "this part" (83.55).

## If the tenant already paid it

"if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (83.56(5)(a)), the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).

Ask what they knew when they paid, and set it beside "actual knowledge" (83.56(5)(a)). Whether paying a raised rent gives up the extra, or changes the rent from then on, is not settled, so going back to the lease's rent and getting the extra back are not settled either. Start the answer there. One: paying with knowledge gives up a suit over those months and may show the tenant agreed. The other: an increase the lease never allowed is not rent "due" (83.43(12)), a clause requiring a signed change still stands, and the extra can be claimed under 83.55, with each later month a "subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool; do not total them.

## If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent

- **A written demand.** "If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(3)). This tool does not count those days; the demand states them. Say not to ignore it.
- **Taking the old rent.** A landlord "does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." (83.56(5)(a)). So taking it does not mean the landlord gave in. "If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must:" (83.56(5)(a)) give a receipt with the date, the amount, and the balance before filing; or put the amount in the court's registry on filing; or post a new 3-day notice (83.56(5)(a)). Whether the lease's rent is "partial" at all is the dispute.
- **No court case, no removal.** "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)). The landlord "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)).
- **A case filed.** Say this first. The tenant must pay into the registry "the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)), and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment removing the tenant (83.60(2)). When the amount is what they dispute, the motion is the way to say so, with papers showing why the amount in the complaint is wrong (83.60(2)). A tenant with subsidized rent deposits only their own share (83.60(2)). Give the 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them; the summons states the requirement (83.60(2)).
- **Defenses.** The tenant "may raise any other defense, whether legal or equitable, that he or she may have, including the defense of retaliatory conduct in accordance with s. 83.64" (83.60(1)(a)). The winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying a landlord may raise the rent during a set term with no clause and no agreement, or calling the lease's own rent steps an increase.
- Treating 83.57's 30 days as settled for an increase, saying flatly that no notice is needed, or saying flatly that a letter alone changes the rent with no set end date.
- Saying an increase is retaliation because it followed a complaint, or leaving out good faith or being treated differently.
- Telling a tenant they can stop paying rent altogether, explaining a case without 83.60(2), or giving a calendar date for its 5 days.
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

tool_calls.name: get_statute_section
tool_calls.result: 83.64 Retaliatory conduct. — (1) It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant. In order for the tenant to raise the defense of retaliatory conduct, the tenant must have acted in good faith. Examples of conduct for which the landlord may not retaliate include, but are not limited to, situations where: (a) The tenant has complained to a governmental agency charged with responsibility for enforcement of a building, housing, or health code of a suspected violation applicable to the premises; (b) The tenant has organized, encouraged, or participated in a tenant organization; (c) The tenant has complained to the landlord pursuant to s. 83.56 (1); (d) The tenant is a servicemember who has terminated a rental agreement pursuant to s. 83.682 ; (e) The tenant has paid rent to a condominium, cooperative, or homeowners’ association after demand from the association in order to pay the landlord’s obligation to the association; or (f) The tenant has exercised his or her rights under local, state, or federal fair housing laws. (2) Evidence of retaliatory conduct may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession. (3) In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause. Examples of good cause include, but are not limited to, good faith actions for nonpayment of rent, violation of the rental agreement or of reasonable rules, or violation of the terms of this chapter. (4) “Discrimination” under this section means that a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord, which shall be a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct. History. — s. 8, ch. 83-151; s. 450, ch. 95-147; s. 3, ch. 2003-72; s. 15, ch. 2013-136.

tool_calls.name: get_statute_section
tool_calls.result: 83.57 Termination of tenancy without specific term. — A tenancy without a specific duration, as defined in s. 83.46 (2) or (3), may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4), as follows: (1) When the tenancy is from year to year, by giving not less than 60 days’ notice prior to the end of any annual period; (2) When the tenancy is from quarter to quarter, by giving not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any quarterly period; (3) When the tenancy is from month to month, by giving not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period; and (4) When the tenancy is from week to week, by giving not less than 7 days’ notice prior to the end of any weekly period. History. — s. 2, ch. 73-330; s. 3, ch. 81-190; s. 15, ch. 83-217; s. 2, ch. 2023-314.

tool_calls.name: get_statute_section
tool_calls.result: 83.56 Termination of rental agreement. — (1) If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement. If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows: (a) If the landlord’s failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable. (b) If the landlord’s failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance. (2) If the tenant materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations, the landlord may: (a) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it or if the noncompliance constitutes a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance and the landlord’s intent to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of noncompliance which are of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure include, but are not limited to, destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act; an act of fraudulent entry of a residential dwelling unit which violates s. 817.537 (2), regardless of whether criminal proceedings have commenced; or a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance. In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately. You shall have 7 days from the delivery of this letter to vacate the premises. This action is taken because (cite the noncompliance) . (b) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance, including a notice that, if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of such noncompliance include, but are not limited to, activities in contravention of the lease or this part such as having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles; parking in an unauthorized manner or permitting such parking; or failing to keep the premises clean and sanitary. If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that (cite the noncompliance) . Demand is hereby made that you remedy the noncompliance within 7 days of receipt of this notice or your lease shall be deemed terminated and you shall vacate the premises upon such termination. answer:
You probably don't owe the $300, but you must act fast in the eviction case. Your lease says $1,050 a month, and you never signed or agreed to $1,200. The lease can be changed only in a signed writing, so your landlord can't raise the rent alone during the lease term. The law gives you only 5 days (not counting Saturdays, Sundays, and court holidays) after you were served to do one of two things. You can pay the rent the complaint claims into the court, or you can file a motion asking the court to decide how much rent is owed. If you do neither, you give up most of your defenses and can be evicted by default. Your "I paid what the lease says" argument may count as a payment defense, which the deadline may not cover. That is not settled, so don't rely on it. The summons should state the requirement. Keep paying the $1,050 on time while the case is open.

Have you filed anything with the court or paid any money into the court yet?

DETAILS

### Is the rent $1,050 or $1,200?
- Your lease says: "Rent is $1,050.00 per month, due on the first day of each month" (lease §4). The lease term runs from August 1, 2025 to July 31, 2026 (§3).
- The new rent was to start March 1, 2026. That date falls inside the lease term, which ends July 31, 2026.
- Florida's landlord-tenant law (ch. 83, part II) has no section that lets a landlord raise rent during a fixed term.
- Your lease has no clause that lets the landlord raise rent mid-term. It says it "may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant" (§10).
- You confirmed that nothing was signed and that you never agreed.
- You never paid the higher rent. The office accepted $1,050 every month, including May.
- So on these facts the rent through July 31, 2026 is $1,050. A court makes the final decision.

### What does the $300 demand mean?
- You told me you received a written demand for $300 on April 20, 2026. The law lets a landlord end a tenancy if rent goes unpaid for 3 days (not counting weekends and court holidays) after a written demand (83.56(3)). That is why the demand matters.
- That demand only works if you actually owe rent. If the lease rent is $1,050 and you paid it, there is nothing unpaid.
- Your landlord may say your $1,050 payments were "partial rent." The law says a landlord "does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period" (83.56(5)(a)). So accepting your payments doesn't end the dispute.
- Whether $1,050 is partial rent is the exact question in dispute. That depends on what the lease rent is, which favors you.

### What must you do now that you've been sued?
- The rule is in 83.60(2). If you raise "any defense other than payment," you must pay into the court registry "the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due."
- You can instead file a motion to determine rent. The law says: "If a motion to determine rent is filed, documentation in support of the allegation that the rent as alleged in the complaint is in error is required." Your lease and your proof of each $1,050 payment are that documentation.
- The deadline is "within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process" (83.60(2)). You were served May 5, 2026.
- Missing it "constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant's defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing" (83.60(2)). A writ of possession is the court order that lets the sheriff remove you.
- A court must also refuse to set mediation or trial until this is done (83.56(5)(b)).
- The motion filing is how you tell the court the amount is wrong.
- Keep paying rent as it comes due. This includes the next month's rent. Which amount you must pay into the registry as rent accrues is something the court can settle in the motion.
- The court forms and the exact steps are outside what this tool covers.

### Can you also raise other defenses?
- Yes. You "may raise any other defense, whether legal or equitable" (83.60(1)(a)). Here, that means the lease sets the rent and no valid demand exists for unpaid rent.
- The winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48).

Read the whole lease, addenda included, for: the rent, the term, any clause on the rent changing, how the lease may be changed, any charges, staying after the end, and how notices go to the landlord. Quote each clause and cite it.

The rent stays where it is for now and the tenant keeps paying it, but the landlord can still raise it by meeting the clause, so say that too. Option 1's plain answer is for a lease with no such clause. A clause with no limit at all: say what it says, that it carries "an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement." - **A new charge** (an amenity fee, a trash fee): the same questions as for rent. The lease provides it: owed as the lease says. It does not: during a set term the landlord cannot add it alone, any more than it can raise the rent. A fee counts as rent only if it is "designated as rent in a written rental agreement." (83.43(12)). That matters because a demand under 83.56(3) and the registry under 83.60(2) speak of rent.
  - Trash: in a unit other than a single-family home or duplex, "Garbage removal and outside receptacles therefor." (83.51(2)(a)) falls to the landlord "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)), though the rental agreement may put the charges on the tenant (83.51(2)(e)).

Whether paying a raised rent gives up the extra, or changes the rent from then on, is not settled, so going back to the lease's rent and getting the extra back are not settled either. Start the answer there. One: paying with knowledge gives up a suit over those months and may show the tenant agreed. The other: an increase the lease never allowed is not rent "due" (83.43(12)), a clause requiring a signed change still stands, and the extra can be claimed under 83.55, with each later month a "subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool; do not total them.

## If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent

- **A written demand.** "If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(3)). This tool does not count those days; the demand states them. Say not to ignore it.
- **Taking the old rent.** A landlord "does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." (83.56(5)(a)). So taking it does not mean the landlord gave in. "If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must:" (83.56(5)(a)) give a receipt with the date, the amount, and the balance before filing; or put the amount in the court's registry on filing; or post a new 3-day notice (83.56(5)(a)). Whether the lease's rent is "partial" at all is the dispute.
- **No court case, no removal.** "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)). The landlord "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)).
- **A case filed.** Say this first. The tenant must pay into the registry "the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)), and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment removing the tenant (83.60(2)). When the amount is what they dispute, the motion is the way to say so, with papers showing why the amount in the complaint is wrong (83.60(2)). A tenant with subsidized rent deposits only their own share (83.60(2)). Give the 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them; the summons states the requirement (83.60(2)).
- **Defenses.** The tenant "may raise any other defense, whether legal or equitable, that he or she may have, including the defense of retaliatory conduct in accordance with s. 83.64" (83.60(1)(a)). The winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying a landlord may raise the rent during a set term with no clause and no agreement, or calling the lease's own rent steps an increase.
- Treating 83.57's 30 days as settled for an increase, saying flatly that no notice is needed, or saying flatly that a letter alone changes the rent with no set end date.
- Saying an increase is retaliation because it followed a complaint, or leaving out good faith or being treated differently.
- Telling a tenant they can stop paying rent altogether, explaining a case without 83.60(2), or giving a calendar date for its 5 days.
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

answer:
It's not settled whether you can go back to $1,050 and get the extra back, because you already paid $1,150 for two months. Your lease sets the rent at $1,050 through July 31, 2026. It says changes must be in writing and signed by both sides, and you signed nothing. Part II of the law has no section that lets a landlord raise rent in the middle of a lease. Paying the higher amount while knowing it was higher may have cost you some rights, though, and the law doesn't clearly say how much. If you go back to $1,050, your landlord could treat the $100 shortfall as unpaid rent and send a written demand. Don't ignore a demand if one comes.

Did you ever tell your landlord yes to the new rent, in person, by text, or by email? Or did you just start paying?

DETAILS

### What does your lease say about the rent and changing it?
- Clause 3 sets the term: "begins on August 1, 2025 and ends on July 31, 2026." The new rent was to start March 1, 2026, so it falls inside the term.
- Clause 4 says: "Rent is $1,050.00 per month, due on the first day of each month."
- Clause 10 says the lease "may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant."
- The lease has no clause that lets the landlord raise rent during the term.
- Part II also has no section that sets a notice period for a rent increase or caps how much rent can go up. Local rules can't add one either (83.425).
- Because of this, the landlord can't change the rent alone before July 31, 2026. A higher rent could apply to a new term after that date, but only if you agree.

### Did paying $1,150 change anything?
This is the unsettled part. Both readings are open.
- **Reading one, against you:** Under 83.56(5)(a), if a tenant "pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord," the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." You told me you knew the amount was higher when you paid, but you hadn't read the lease. A court could treat those two payments as given up. It could also treat paying as showing you accepted the new amount.
- **Reading two, for you:** An increase the lease never allowed isn't rent that is "due" (83.43(12)). Clause 10 still requires a signed change. Under 83.55, a party hurt when the other side doesn't follow "the requirements of the rental agreement or this part" may "recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." Each later month the landlord demands the higher rent would be a new "subsequent or continuing noncompliance" under 83.56(5)(a), so paying earlier wouldn't bar a claim for those months.
- Whether you can recover the extra, the amount, and the court steps are outside what I can work out here.

### What if you pay $1,050 and your landlord objects?
- Under 83.56(3), if rent isn't paid when due and a written demand goes unpaid for 3 days (not counting Saturday, Sunday, or court holidays), the landlord "may terminate the rental agreement." Your landlord would say the $100 is unpaid rent. You would say it was never owed.
- If your landlord accepts $1,050, that doesn't mean the landlord gave in. Under 83.56(5)(a), accepting "partial rent" doesn't waive the landlord's rights. Whether $1,050 counts as partial rent is the disagreement.
- Your landlord can't remove you without a court case (83.59(3)), and can't block your access to the apartment (83.67(2)).
- If your landlord files a case, you must pay the rent into the court's registry, or file a motion about the amount, within 5 days (not counting Saturdays, Sundays, or court holidays) after being served. Missing that waives your defenses other than payment, and can lead to a default judgment (83.60(2)). The summons will state the requirement.

### How could you object in writing?
- You can tell your landlord in writing that you don't agree to the increase. Quote clauses 4 and 10.
- Clause 7 says notices to the landlord must be "delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, Gainesville, Florida 32608, or sent there by certified mail."
- Keep a copy of the letter, your lease, and proof of each payment.

Loaded rent_increased. Its instructions:

# Rent increased

Rests on 83.46 (rent, tenancies with no set term), 83.43 (what rent is, good faith), 83.57 (ending a tenancy with no set term), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.425 (local rules), 83.56 (unpaid rent, rent paid, notices), 83.60 (if sued), 83.55 and 83.54 (damages, suits), 83.44 and 83.45 (good faith, unfair clauses), 83.48 (attorney fees), 83.51 and 83.491 (trash, a fee in place of a deposit), 83.59 and 83.67 (no lockout), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes"). Every point marked not settled gets all its readings, and you choose none. When the tenant asks "can I" and the answer turns on such a point, write "You can if X, and X is not settled", never a plain yes.

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- Part II has no section that sets how much notice a rent increase needs, and none that limits how much rent may go up. Say so plainly when asked. Never state a notice period or a cap as the law.
- Local rules: "The regulation of residential tenancies, the landlord-tenant relationship, and all other matters covered under this part are preempted to the state." (83.425), and the section supersedes local rules on matters including "fees charged by the landlord; or notice requirements." (83.425). The stored text holds no local rent rule. Never apply one from memory.
- Rent paid through a program (a voucher, public housing): the program's own rules are not stored. Say they may limit this, and that they are outside this tool.
- The increase comes with an offer to renew, or the tenant would rather leave: load lease_ending too.

## What the lease adds

Read the whole lease, addenda included, for: the rent, the term, any clause on the rent changing, how the lease may be changed, any charges, staying after the end, and how notices go to the landlord. Quote each clause and cite it.

- **Rent steps set in the lease from the start** (so much until a date, then more): that is the lease's rent, not an increase. Say so.
- **A clause letting the landlord raise the rent during the term:** set the increase beside the clause's conditions (how much notice, how it is given, how much, how often). If it gives a number of days N: the last day to give notice for the start date named is count_days(new_rent_starts, -N), and the earliest start from the notice given is count_days(increase_delivered, N). All conditions met: the rent goes up as the lease says; say so plainly. Any not met: the clause does not support this increase on these terms; say so plainly. The rent stays where it is for now and the tenant keeps paying it, but the landlord can still raise it by meeting the clause, so say that too. Option 1's plain answer is for a lease with no such clause. A clause with no limit at all: say what it says, that it carries "an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement." (83.44), and that whether it is unfair enough to be "unconscionable" (83.45(1)) is for a court.
- **A new charge** (an amenity fee, a trash fee): the same questions as for rent. The lease provides it: owed as the lease says. It does not: during a set term the landlord cannot add it alone, any more than it can raise the rent. A fee counts as rent only if it is "designated as rent in a written rental agreement." (83.43(12)). That matters because a demand under 83.56(3) and the registry under 83.60(2) speak of rent.
  - Trash: in a unit other than a single-family home or duplex, "Garbage removal and outside receptacles therefor." (83.51(2)(a)) falls to the landlord "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)), though the rental agreement may put the charges on the tenant (83.51(2)(e)).
  - A fee in place of a security deposit: "The amount of the fee, which may not be increased during the term of the rental agreement." (83.491(4)(a)).

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- new_rent: the new amount. increase_delivered: the date word of it reached them, and how it came (handed over, mail, portal, text, spoken). new_rent_starts: the date it is said to start.
- lease_end_date: the date the lease ends, if it has one. period_end: the last day of the rent period before the new rent starts. next_period_end: the last day of the rent period after that.
- agreed: whether they signed anything or said yes. paid_new_rent: whether they have paid the new amount, for which months, and what they knew about the lease when they paid.
- complaint_date: the date of any complaint or similar step before the increase, and what it was. others_rent: what they know about other tenants' rent.
- rent_demand: any written demand for rent, and its date. eviction_filed: whether a case has been filed, and whether they were served.

## Which kind of increase

Settle this first. With a set end date, call count_days(lease_end_date, 0) and set new_rent_starts beside the date it gives.

- A set end date, and the new rent starts on or before it: option 1.
- A set end date, and the new rent starts after it: option 2.
- No set end date, or the tenant stayed on after a set term with the landlord's permission: option 3. With no term stated, "the duration is determined by the periods for which the rent is payable." (83.46(2)). Stayed on without permission, or in doubt: load lease_ending too.

Any kind: option 4 if the tenant did something first that the landlord may be answering, such as a complaint or joining a tenant group, and the two parts after it if they fit.

## Option 1: during a set term

Part II has no section that lets a landlord raise the rent during a set term. The rent is what the lease says. Quote the rent clause and any clause on changing the lease.

1. **No clause allows it** (see "What the lease adds").
2. **The tenant did not agree.**
   - They signed a change: the rent is what they signed, if it meets the lease's clause on changes.
   - They said yes without signing: not settled whether that changes the rent. One: a rental agreement can include an "oral agreement for a duration of less than 1 year" (83.43(13)). The other: a lease clause requiring a signed change still governs.
   - They paid it without signing: this option's plain answer does not apply. Start from "If the tenant already paid it", which is not settled.

Both met: the landlord cannot change the rent alone before the lease ends. Say so plainly. The tenant keeps paying the lease's rent, in full and on time, and can tell the landlord in writing that they do not agree, quoting the rent clause and sending it the way the lease's notice clause says. It helps to keep the letter, the lease, and proof of each payment. Say the risk too: see "If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent". The landlord can ask for more when the term ends (option 2).

## Option 2: a higher rent for a new term

Part II names no right to renew at the same rent and no limit on what a landlord may ask for a new term. Say so plainly. The lease's rent stands through lease_end_date whatever the offer says. From there:

- **Agree:** the new rent starts with the new term. Say what they should read before signing: the rent, the term, and any new charge.
- **Leave at the end:** load lease_ending for any notice the lease asks for.
- **Stay without agreeing:** load lease_ending. Staying without permission can mean "double the amount of rent due" (83.58). Read the lease's clause on staying after the end; if it makes the tenancy month to month, say what it says, and option 3 applies from then.

## Option 3: no set end date

Part II sets no notice for this and does not say a landlord may change the rent alone, so what an increase takes is not settled. Give all three readings and choose none. Quote any lease clause on signed changes.

- One: a landlord that can end the tenancy only on 83.57's notice can change the rent only with the same notice, written and delivered a way 83.56(4) names, for month to month "not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)).
- Two: no section sets a notice, so none in particular is needed, and the tenant can pay it or leave.
- Three: 83.57 only lets a party end the tenancy, so the rent changes only if the tenant agrees, and a landlord that wants more must end the tenancy on that notice and offer new terms.

The date: count_days(period_end, -N), with N from 83.57: 30 for month to month (83.57(3)), and for other rent periods the number in 83.57(1), (2), or (4). Set increase_delivered beside it. The ways 83.56(4) names are mailing, a true copy by hand, e-mail under the signed addendum in 83.505(1), or, if the tenant is away, a copy left at the home.

- In writing, a way named, and on or before that date: in time under readings one and two. Say so plainly. Under reading three the letter alone still does not change the rent.
- Later than that, or spoken, or by text or portal: not good for that date under reading one, enough under reading two, and no change under reading three. Whether a late notice works for the next period under reading one is not settled, as lease_ending says of a late notice to end a tenancy; its date is count_days(next_period_end, -N).

Under every reading the landlord may end the tenancy on that notice: it "may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4)" (83.57), and no reason is named. Say so, so the tenant knows what refusing can lead to.

The short answer here: say it is not settled, then write "You have three choices, and each has a risk", then name the three below without choosing one. In the details, say what each one risks.

- Pay the new rent. Whether paying gives anything up is not settled; give both readings from "If the tenant already paid it", never one as the law.
- Pay the old rent and say in writing why. See "If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent".
- End the tenancy by written notice. Give the last day here, with the other choices: count_days(period_end, -N), or count_days(next_period_end, -N) if that has passed. Then load lease_ending for how the notice goes.

## Option 4: retaliation

"It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)).

All of these must be met.

1. **Something the tenant did first.** "Examples of conduct for which the landlord may not retaliate include, but are not limited to, situations where:" (83.64(1)) they complained to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)), took part in a tenant organization (83.64(1)(b)), complained to the landlord under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)), ended a lease as a servicemember (83.64(1)(d)), paid rent to an association after its demand (83.64(1)(e)), or used fair housing rights (83.64(1)(f)). Fair housing law itself is outside this tool. Another step, like an ordinary repair request: not settled. One: the list is only examples, so it can count. The other: it counts only if it is like the named ones, and a request that says nothing about ending the lease is not 83.56(1)'s complaint.
2. **Good faith** (83.64(1)). "“Good faith” means honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned." (83.43(8)). Applying that is for a court.
3. **Treated differently.** "“Discrimination” under this section means that a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord, which shall be a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct." (83.64(4)). Set what they know of other tenants' rent beside the words. The same increase for everyone points against it; say so plainly. If they do not know, say that is the fact to find out.
4. **Primarily to retaliate.** This is the landlord's motive, for a court. An increase that followed such a step is not retaliation for that reason alone. Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

What it gives: "Evidence of retaliatory conduct may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." (83.64(2)), unless "the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)), whose examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)). So not paying the new rent can weaken it; say so.

What the tenant can do about an increase alone, before any case: not settled. One: 83.64(2) makes it only a defense, so there is nothing to raise until a case. The other: 83.64(1) makes the increase unlawful, "Any right or duty declared in this part is enforceable by civil action." (83.54), and a party may recover damages for a failure to comply with "this part" (83.55).

## If the tenant already paid it

"if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (83.56(5)(a)), the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).

Ask what they knew when they paid, and set it beside "actual knowledge" (83.56(5)(a)). Whether paying a raised rent gives up the extra, or changes the rent from then on, is not settled, so going back to the lease's rent and getting the extra back are not settled either. Start the answer there. One: paying with knowledge gives up a suit over those months and may show the tenant agreed. The other: an increase the lease never allowed is not rent "due" (83.43(12)), a clause requiring a signed change still stands, and the extra can be claimed under 83.55, with each later month a "subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool; do not total them.

## If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent

- **A written demand.** "If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(3)). This tool does not count those days; the demand states them. Say not to ignore it.
- **Taking the old rent.** A landlord "does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." (83.56(5)(a)). So taking it does not mean the landlord gave in. "If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must:" (83.56(5)(a)) give a receipt with the date, the amount, and the balance before filing; or put the amount in the court's registry on filing; or post a new 3-day notice (83.56(5)(a)). Whether the lease's rent is "partial" at all is the dispute.
- **No court case, no removal.** "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)). The landlord "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)).
- **A case filed.** Say this first. The tenant must pay into the registry "the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)), and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment removing the tenant (83.60(2)). When the amount is what they dispute, the motion is the way to say so, with papers showing why the amount in the complaint is wrong (83.60(2)). A tenant with subsidized rent deposits only their own share (83.60(2)). Give the 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them; the summons states the requirement (83.60(2)).
- **Defenses.** The tenant "may raise any other defense, whether legal or equitable, that he or she may have, including the defense of retaliatory conduct in accordance with s. 83.64" (83.60(1)(a)). The winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying a landlord may raise the rent during a set term with no clause and no agreement, or calling the lease's own rent steps an increase.
- Treating 83.57's 30 days as settled for an increase, saying flatly that no notice is needed, or saying flatly that a letter alone changes the rent with no set end date.
- Saying an increase is retaliation because it followed a complaint, or leaving out good faith or being treated differently.
- Telling a tenant they can stop paying rent altogether, explaining a case without 83.60(2), or giving a calendar date for its 5 days.
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

answer:
You don't owe the $300 under your lease, but you have a short deadline in the court case, so act now. Your lease sets rent at $1,050 through July 31, 2026, and you never agreed to $1,200. Your landlord can't raise the rent alone during the lease. That is the main defense to the $300 claim. If you do nothing within 5 court days of being served (weekends and court holidays don't count), you can lose that defense and the court can order you out without a hearing. Get the paperwork in on time, either by paying into the court or by filing a motion that says the amount is wrong. I'd also talk to a lawyer or legal aid quickly, because I can't tell you which filing fits your summons.

Have you paid any money into the court or filed anything yet?

DETAILS

### Does your lease allow the rent to go up to $1,200?
- No. Part II of the statute has no section that lets a landlord raise rent during a fixed lease term. Your lease runs to July 31, 2026, and the $1,200 was to start March 1, 2026, which is inside that term.
- Lease §4 says: "Rent is $1,050.00 per month." Nothing in the lease lets the landlord raise it mid-term.
- Lease §10 says the lease "may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant." You told me nothing was signed.
- So the lease rent is still $1,050. A landlord could ask for more rent for a new term after July 31, 2026, but not before.

### Does the landlord's acceptance of $1,050 matter?
- Under 83.56(5)(a), a landlord "does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period."
- Your landlord may argue your $1,050 payments were "partial" rent. Your answer is that $1,050 was the full rent due, so nothing was owed.
- If the landlord took partial rent after posting a nonpayment notice, it had to do one of three things before filing: give you a receipt showing the balance, put that amount into the court registry, or post a new 3-day notice (83.56(5)(a)). The May payment was accepted, so ask whether any of these was done.

### What is the deadline in the eviction case?
- Under 83.60(2), if you raise any defense other than payment, you must pay into the court registry "the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due."
- You must either do that or "file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process." You were served May 5, 2026. The summons should state the requirement.
- The risk is that missing this "constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant's defenses other than payment." The landlord then gets "an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession."
- Because you dispute the amount, a motion to determine rent is the way to say so. It must include documents showing the complaint's amount is wrong (83.60(2)). Your lease and your proof of each $1,050 payment are the documents to use.
- Whether your defense counts as "payment" is something I can't settle. That is why I'd get legal help to choose the safest filing.
- If you're in subsidized housing, you deposit only your own share (83.60(2)).

### What if the landlord just locks you out?
- It can't. A landlord "shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except" through a court case, or if the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)).
- A landlord also "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)).

### Can you recover costs?
- In a case like this, the winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48).
- You may also raise "any other defense, whether legal or equitable" (83.60(1)(a)).
- The 3-day demand dated April 20, 2026, must also meet 83.56(3). I haven't seen it, so I can't say whether it does.
